verses.14:
Al-Mizan presents this Meccan sūrah as affirming al-qiyāmat al-kubrā, the greater resurrection, whose signs, human reckoning, death as the passage to the hereafter, and final proof from original creation form its course. A translator distinguishes this from the individual, lesser resurrection, al-qiyāmat al-ṣughrā. The oaths by the Day and the self-blaming soul have the omitted force, ‘You will certainly be resurrected’; whether lā uqsimu is the oath as a whole, lā is zāʾidah, or it negates in order to magnify the Day, the result is an oath. The translator also records a possible double function for lā: arresting attention and refuting a prevailing belief. The self-blaming soul may be the believer’s profitable reproach for sin and slack obedience, the disbeliever’s remorse at resurrection, or every human soul’s self-censure according to its condition.

The rhetorical question about assembling bones rebukes denial of resurrection. God can restore even the former precise form of the banānahu, the fingertips; making fingers and toes equal like hooves is considered less plausible. Al-Mizan reads bal in (75:5) as correcting the alleged doubt about divine power: denial arises because people want continuing fujūr, the tearing of piety’s curtain, in their future, rather than faith and taqwā. Their question about the Day is therefore derisive denial, not responsible preparation; the reported Prophetic maxim that what must come is near reinforces this. Dazzled eyes, the moon’s lost light, and the sun and moon brought together are signs of the Hour. The guilty cry for al-mafarr, a refuge, but God answers that no wazar, sanctuary, exists.

The exclusive recourse to the Lord means an unavoidable journey into His presence, not an escape; the veil in (83:14-15) is exclusion from grace and mercy, not ignorance of or absence from Him. Al-Mizan records other readings that make the recourse one’s appointed abode or God’s judgment. What a person ‘sent ahead and left behind’ may mean earlier and later deeds, or deeds before death together with the continuing effects of a good or evil practice; other proposed distributions of deeds, neglected duties, and possessions are rejected as remote. Bal then replaces external information with the person’s own intensified baṣīrah, inward awareness, or, on another reading, proof against himself through the testimony of his faculties. Excuses, or even covers concealing deeds, cannot defeat that self-witness.

The sūrah’s opening and its ominous scenes thus establish certain resurrection, human accountability, and the futility of denial motivated by attachment to sin.

verses.40:
Al-Mizan reads (75:16-19) as a parenthetical instruction to the Prophet, independent of the resurrection discussion: when revelation is being given, he must not anticipate its recitation, but remain quiet until it is complete. The pronouns concern the Qur’an or revelation; God undertakes its collection and recitation, then its bayānah, exposition, in that sequence. This accords with (20:114). Narrations that the Qur’an was revealed first all at once and later gradually are said to support the prohibition on hastening. Al-Mizan prefers collection of the revealed parts and God’s recitation to the alternative that God preserves all meanings in the Prophet’s heart and affirms recitation on his tongue; it accepts that ‘follow its recitation’ may mean silent, attentive listening, but rejects readings that make it obedience to commands or private repetition. An alternative understanding of bayānah as communicating the message to people is recorded.

It rejects the view that the Prophet was merely fearing forgetfulness, since the order is not to hasten and to follow only after recitation. It also rejects readings that make the passage the sinner’s hurried reading of his record on the Day, or an injunction not to ask when resurrection will come: a parenthesis needs no connection to its neighbors, and the Qur’anic parallel (20:114) itself occurs amid resurrection discourse.

The address then returns to all people. Kallā rejects the assumption that bones will not be reassembled, while bal identifies love of the immediate worldly life and neglect of the hereafter as the real motive. On the Day, radiant, satisfied faces contrast with intensely scowling faces that know a crushing punishment awaits. Al-Mizan denies physical vision of God and reads looking toward the Lord as the heart’s vision through faith, supported by rational proof and reports from the Infallibles under (7:143) and (53:11). The blessed remain oriented to Him through every paradise pleasure because they see every thing as His sign; a sign does not veil what it signifies. The word order therefore indicates their constant orientation, not a rhyme-based or intermittent exclusivity. A translator’s note records a more apparent reading of naẓar as intiẓār, expectation of good from the Lord, confirmed by a hadith and later accepted by the author.

Kallā at death warns those who prefer the world: the soul reaches the collarbones and the family’s call for a rāq, a healer, expresses despair; the alternative is angels asking whether mercy or punishment will raise the soul. The dying person knows this is separation from the world. Though the apparent intertwining of the shanks describes bodily death, Al-Mizan finds it more plausibly a succession of calamities from death to resurrection, incorporating readings about the two worlds and their terrors. Al-masāq is the compulsory driving to God, whose final exclusivity is preferred over readings that introduce an omitted judgment or promised abode, or turn God into merely the driver.

The person who rejects the Qur’anic call has failed both its roots, by not confirming truth, and its practical branch, by not praying; he turns away and swaggeringly returns to his family. Al-Mizan tentatively reads the repeated awlā laka as God’s curse on such qualities and their consequences: the sealing of the heart against faith and taqwā and a decree of hell. The many etymological and elliptical alternatives are contrived, though the reading that the Fire is most fitting comes close. The closing rhetorical question rejects the notion that humanity is sudā, neglected and without obligation or requital; a translator notes a secondary application to existential forlornness and angst. Human development from emitted semen to clinging mass, fashioned male and female, establishes that the Creator’s original act proves His power to revive the dead, a restoration no harder than creation itself.
